details.title: Google Glass Enterprise Edition 2

entry_date.label: By May 2019
entry_date.basis: Google dates launch to May; 20 May begins contact with sales/partners and a 21 May trade report says partner availability.

details.detailText:
By May 2019

Google Glass Enterprise Edition 2

Technology · United States; Taiwan

Google Glass Enterprise Edition 2, model GG2; enterprise assisted-reality wearable. Excludes Explorer Edition and Enterprise Edition 1.

Optics & glass
Materials

Why this date

Available for purchase by May 2019. Community: Enterprise customers purchasing through Google’s sales or partner channel. Google dates launch to May; 20 May begins contact with sales/partners and a 21 May trade report says partner availability.

The mark is an upper date limit for the stated entry claim. Earlier entry remains unresolved.

Direct evidence.

The May 2019 enterprise-channel offer and 21 May partner-availability report support availability by that time; direct developer resellers came later in 2020.

The event is month-precision and does not prove first transaction, availability in every market, or direct reseller purchase in May 2019.

Scope: regions unspecified. Applications: Hands-free enterprise work. Population: not yet researched. Market: Businesses purchasing through solution partners.

Scoped configuration: Glass Enterprise Edition 2 partner offer reported in May 2019; first commercial-offer date not established.

First commercial availability: unknown; applicability: applicable.

Historical claim: accepted. Lifecycle classification: accepted.

A May 2019 enterprise partner offer and a February 2020 direct-reseller offer are documented. Purchase quantities and the dates of first offers are unknown; prior private arrangements were not excluded.

Entry evidence

Glass Enterprise Edition 2: faster and more helpful · 20 May 2019, final paragraph

Invites businesses to contact sales or solution partners starting that day.

Google Glass Enterprise Edition 2 resurrects AR for Google · 21 May 2019, final paragraph

Reports EE2 available for business through third-party partners with MSRP $999.

Glass Enterprise Edition 2 now available for developers · 4 February 2020, second paragraph

Dates launch to previous May and describes a new direct reseller channel for developers.

Lifecycle dates and unknowns
Recorded events

commercial offer · May 2019

Google announced Glass Enterprise Edition 2 on 20 May 2019 and invited enterprise customers to contact its sales team or partners; a 21 May report described partner availability.

commercial offer · 4 February 2020

On 4 February 2020 Google said developers and businesses could purchase Glass Enterprise Edition 2 devices directly from named hardware resellers.

withdrawal · By 15 March 2023

By 15 March 2023 Google was no longer selling Glass Enterprise Edition, including Edition 2; reseller withdrawal and last actual device use are not established.

support end · 15 September 2023

Google identified a support and replacement cutoff for Glass Enterprise Edition.

documented description · 8 August 2018

The test laboratory received a Glass Enterprise Edition 2 GG2 sample.

Sources

Glass Enterprise Edition 2 now available for developers (2020)
About Glass Enterprise Edition 2 (date not stated)

Google Glass Enterprise Edition 2 resurrects AR for Google (2019)

B-DNA helical constraints

Science · King’s College London, England

Awareness proxy

Franklin and Gosling inferred a probable helix, approximately 34 Å repeat and 20 Å diameter, with exterior phosphates and a probable two-chain unit.

Genetics

Built on
Humidity-varied DNA diffraction
1953

Hydration-dependent fibre diffraction supplied the patterns from which Franklin and Gosling inferred B-form geometry.

Linked events: demonstration (by 1953) → dated assertion (by Apr 1953).

Earlier exposures and subsequent interpretation overlap in the evidence; the inference was documented by 1953, without an established date of first formulation.

The Nature paper exposed the qualified inferences to the structural-biology literature rather than using the earlier undated inference.

The article is a documented route to specialist awareness; later adoption of this exact bundle was not established.

Publication does not prove other scientists agreed with every part, nor establish earliest external exposure.

Scope: regions unspecified. Applications: unspecified. Population: not yet researched. Market: not yet researched.

First commercial availability: not applicable; applicability: not applicable.

Historical claim: accepted. Lifecycle classification: needs review.

The authors did not call diffraction alone direct proof of helicity or offer a complete structure; the model involved additional density and chemical arguments.

details.title: Photolithographic diffusion windows

entry_date.label: By 1958
entry_date.basis: Latest documented community-use or recognition bound; no earliest date is established.

details.detailText:
By 1958

Photolithographic diffusion windows

Technology · Bell Laboratories, New Jersey, United States

Scoped inference

Jules Andrus and Walter Bond adapted photoresist patterning to etch windows in silicon oxide before localized diffusion.

Semiconductors

Built on
Silicon oxide diffusion mask
By 1955

Andrus and Bond applied photoresist patterning to Frosch and Derick’s oxide-mask process.

Linked events: dated assertion (1955) → dated assertion (1955).

Both nodes are 1955; the source states the dependency, so year-level overlap is not a reversed chronology.

Why this date

Use contextually inferred by 1958. Community: Fairchild mesa-transistor fabrication engineers. Latest documented community-use or recognition bound; no earliest date is established.

The mark is an upper date limit for the stated entry claim. Earlier entry remains unresolved.

Scoped contextual inference.

Moore’s contemporary-participant account connects Fairchild photolithography, oxide-masked mesa emitters and 1958 shipments, providing earlier real specialist use than the 1964 patent.

The dated use follows from linked passages on the Fairchild process and 1958 shipments; it does not assert identical Bell masks or an independently demonstrated first use.

The Fairchild method is contextual evidence of use of the same general patterned oxide-window process; the source does not identify every original Bell mask or prove exact transfer of a physical tool.

Scope: California, United States. Applications: transistor emitter diffusion. Population: not yet researched. Market: not yet researched.

Scoped configuration: Fairchild’s photoresist-patterned silicon-oxide openings used to delimit diffusion in mesa transistor fabrication; individual masks need not be identical to the earlier Bell Labs masks.

First commercial availability: not yet researched; applicability: not yet assessed.

Historical claim: accepted. Lifecycle classification: needs review.

This node is not Fairchild’s later step-and-repeat camera or DOFL’s separate diode-array work.

Entry evidence

The Role of Fairchild in Silicon Technology · Printed pp. 54–58, photolithography, early mesa transistors and oxide-masked emitter diffusion

Moore describes photoresist and oxide openings, Fairchild’s mesa emitter diffusion, and 100 early 2N696 shipments in 1958.

Lifecycle dates and unknowns
Recorded events

dated assertion · 1955

Jules Andrus and Walter Bond adapted photoresist patterning to etch windows in silicon oxide before localized diffusion.

publication · 1964-03-03

Andrus issued patent publicly described photoresist-patterned windows in silicon oxide for selective diffusion.

practical use · by 1958

Fairchild used photolithographic oxide-window fabrication in its mesa transistor work and shipped 100 2N696 transistors by 1958.

details.title: Greco-Roman common-measure procedure

entry_date.label: By approximately 325
entry_date.basis: The source dates Iamblichus’s death to approximately 325 CE; this estimated upper bound is not a precisely known death or writing date, and the earlier bound is unknown.

details.detailText:
By approximately 325

Greco-Roman common-measure procedure

Science · Eastern Mediterranean

Greco-Roman numerical common-measure procedure using alternating subtraction, represented by Euclid Elements VII.2 and the later odd-number accounts of Nicomachus and Iamblichus.

Mathematics
Arithmetic

Why this date

In use by approximately 325. Community: Iamblichus, as a scholarly commentator on Nicomachus. The source dates Iamblichus’s death to approximately 325 CE; this estimated upper bound is not a precisely known death or writing date, and the earlier bound is unknown.

The mark is an upper date limit for the stated entry claim. Earlier entry remains unresolved.

Direct evidence.

A named later scholar explained the same numerical procedure and gave an example, providing specific scholarly reception centuries before the 888 manuscript. The earlier Nicomachus description remains separately recorded.

The sources do not establish when or where this numerical procedure was first used, that Nicomachus or Iamblichus read Euclid VII.2 directly, or that either consulted the later 888 Bodleian manuscript. Iamblichus’s life dates and the chronology of his commentary are approximate; his explicit example concerns two odd numbers.

Scope: regions unspecified. Applications: scholarly exposition and a numerical example. Population: not yet researched. Market: not yet researched.

Scoped configuration: Iamblichus’s commentary on Nicomachus describes the numerical common-measure procedure for two odd numbers.

First commercial availability: not yet researched; applicability: not applicable.

Historical claim: accepted. Lifecycle classification: needs review.

The sources do not establish when or where this numerical procedure was first used, that Nicomachus or Iamblichus read Euclid VII.2 directly, or that either consulted the later 888 Bodleian manuscript. Iamblichus’s life dates and the chronology of his commentary are approximate; his explicit example concerns two odd numbers.

Entry evidence

The Euclidean Algorithm and Finite Continued Fractions · §12, Iamblichus, Commentary on Nicomachus §§98–99, quoted from Vinel 2014 p. 97

Iamblichus describes alternating subtraction to determine the common measure for two odd numbers and gives a concrete example.

Iamblichus · Opening paragraph and §1.2 Works

Places Iamblichus’s life at approximately 242–325 CE and identifies his mathematical introduction as based on Nicomachus.

Lifecycle dates and unknowns
Recorded events

public availability · 888

Stephen copied a manuscript of the Elements containing the Book VII greatest-common-measure proposition.

documented description · By approximately the first half of the second century CE

Nicomachus described the numerical common-measure method in his Introduction to Arithmetic.

practical use · By approximately 325 CE

Iamblichus explained the common-measure method in his scholarly treatment of Nicomachus, including an odd-number example.

Sources
Euclid’s Elements, Bodleian Euclid (2008)
Euclid’s Elements, Book VII (2008)
The Euclidean Algorithm and Finite Continued Fractions (2023)
Iamblichus (2023)
Pythagoreanism (2024)

details.title: Rhind papyrus worked mathematical text

entry_date.label: About 1650–1550 BCE (different scholarly estimates)
entry_date.basis: Chace’s 1927 edition estimates about 1650 BCE; the modern British Museum exhibition guide estimates about 1550 BCE. These two approximate estimates define the displayed range, not proven chronological limits.

details.detailText:
About 1650–1550 BCE (different scholarly estimates)

Rhind papyrus worked mathematical text

Science · Ancient Egypt

Scoped inference

The mathematical text preserved in the Rhind papyrus: worked problems with arithmetic, fractions and areas, copied by the scribe Aḥmose.

Mathematics
Arithmetic

Why this date

Availability inferred from the stated context. Community: Aḥmose, the copyist. Chace’s 1927 edition estimates about 1650 BCE; the modern British Museum exhibition guide estimates about 1550 BCE. These two approximate estimates define the displayed range, not proven chronological limits.

Scoped contextual inference.

The named scribe had access to a mathematical source for copying.

A copied text implies access to an exemplar by that copyist, not actual performance of each computation or widespread dissemination.

The British Museum estimates about 1550 BCE, while Chace’s older edition gives about 1650 BCE; the competing estimates and approximate range do not establish an exact copying year. The particular copied exemplar is lost; the scribe’s understanding and contemporary readership are not demonstrated.

Scope: regions unspecified. Applications: manuscript copying. Population: not yet researched. Market: not yet researched.

First commercial availability: not yet researched; applicability: not applicable.

Historical claim: accepted. Lifecycle classification: needs review.

The British Museum estimates about 1550 BCE, while Chace’s older edition gives about 1650 BCE; the competing estimates and approximate range do not establish an exact copying year. The particular copied exemplar is lost; the scribe’s understanding and contemporary readership are not demonstrated.

Entry evidence

Hieroglyphs: Unlocking Ancient Egypt, Large Print Guide · Printed p. 144 / PDF p. 144, Textbook maths

Describes the surviving papyrus, its mathematical problems, and approximate date.

Identifies Aḥmose as copyist and discusses uncertainties about comprehension.

details.title: Abū Kāmil’s algebra

entry_date.label: Approximately 1010 CE
entry_date.basis: Tou’s historical presentation dates composition of al-Fakhrī to around 1010; this is an estimate, not a precisely known composition, publication or first-access date.

details.detailText:
Approximately 1010 CE

Abū Kāmil’s algebra

Science · Egypt; Baghdad, Iraq; Maghrib

Scoped inference

Abū Kāmil’s algebraic treatise, the subject of al-Qurashī’s later mathematical commentary.

Mathematics

1 linked entry traces back to this one.

Led to
Al-Qurashī’s algebra commentary
By 1407

Al-Qurashī’s algebra commentary was written on Abū Kāmil’s book.

Node-level textual dependency only; later selected entry events do not assert the date or act of composition.

Why this date

Use inferred from the stated context. Community: Al-Karajī, as the author of al-Fakhrī. Tou’s historical presentation dates composition of al-Fakhrī to around 1010; this is an estimate, not a precisely known composition, publication or first-access date.

Scoped contextual inference.

Karpinski identifies a specific earlier scholarly use in al-Fakhrī than al-Qurashī’s later commentary; the latter event remains preserved.

The historical attribution is a published scholarly reconstruction from parallels, not an explicit citation of Abū Kāmil in al-Fakhrī or an independently inspected original manuscript.

Karpinski’s attribution rests on a historian’s comparison: al-Karajī did not name Abū Kāmil, and the original al-Fakhrī and its Arabic manuscript witnesses were not independently examined for this record. The estimated composition around 1010 is approximate; a modern presentation lists alternative death estimates around 1019 and 1029. None establishes an exact composition day, publication date, or first reception.

Scope: Baghdad, Iraq. Applications: algebraic scholarship in al-Fakhrī. Population: not yet researched. Market: not yet researched.

Scoped configuration: Specific problems and geometrical solutions from Abū Kāmil’s algebra, which Karpinski attributes to al-Karajī’s al-Fakhrī.

First commercial availability: not yet researched; applicability: not applicable.

Historical claim: accepted. Lifecycle classification: needs review.

Karpinski’s attribution rests on a historian’s comparison: al-Karajī did not name Abū Kāmil, and the original al-Fakhrī and its Arabic manuscript witnesses were not independently examined for this record. The estimated composition around 1010 is approximate; a modern presentation lists alternative death estimates around 1019 and 1029. None establishes an exact composition day, publication date, or first reception. Al-Qurashī’s distinct commentary is also known from later testimony and surviving fragments.

Entry evidence

The Algebra of Abu Kamil · Printed p. 38 / PDF p. 3, The Second Great Arabic Writer on Algebra

Karpinski attributes reuse of Abū Kāmil’s algebraic problems and solutions to al-Karajī’s al-Fakhrī; the latter does not name Abū Kāmil.

Abu Bekr ibn Muhammad ibn al-Husayn Al-Karaji · Quick Info; Biography, first four paragraphs

Places al-Fakhrī in Baghdad and estimates al-Karajī’s death around 1029.

Thousand-Year-Old Geometry: Al-Karajī’s Treatise on the Extraction of Hidden Waters · Slide 5 / PDF p. 5, al-Karajī’s Life and Career

Places composition of al-Fakhrī about 1010 and lists alternative death estimates around 1019 and 1029.

Lifecycle dates and unknowns
Recorded events

practical use · By 1184

Al-Qurashī wrote an algebraic commentary on Abū Kāmil’s treatise.

practical use · Approximately 1010 CE

Karpinski identifies al-Karajī’s al-Fakhrī as reusing algebraic problems and solutions from Abū Kāmil’s treatise.

Sources

The Algebra of Abu Kamil (1914)
Abu Bekr ibn Muhammad ibn al-Husayn Al-Karaji (1999)
